Different service lives: compare annual-equivalent cost and the actual replacement calendar

Four charts compare equal-service ownership cycles with different prices and lives, reconcile a common repeated horizon and keep annual valuation separate from the cash needed to buy.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare repeated service cycles with equivalent annual costs

Interactive planning lab

Common service horizon · whole repeated cycles8
Option A · equivalent annual cost$410.59
Option B · equivalent annual cost$347.06

Original hypothetical equal-service comparison, not a product quote, lifespan forecast or personal purchase recommendation. Both options deliver the same required service continuously. Each cycle’s purchase is paid at its start; running cost is paid at every completed year-end for the year just used, including the final service year. Both have zero salvage value. Every later cycle repeats the same purchase price, life and running cost in unchanged nominal CAD; no inflation, technological change, quality difference, downtime, tax, fee, grant or financing is modeled. The entered discount assumption is effective annual and applied to that same unchanging nominal price basis. A cycle’s present cost equals its immediate price plus discounted year-end running costs. Dividing by its own year-end annuity factor gives an equivalent annual cost: a valuation transformation, not a bill, depreciation charge or required saving contribution. The common horizon is the least common multiple of the two whole service lives, at most 56 years under these controls. Each option is replaced at its cycle boundaries before that horizon, with no new purchase at the final endpoint; final service costs still apply. Long repeated horizons make a conditional arithmetic comparison and are not a forecast that today’s prices or technology will persist. No bank balance, affordability, available replacement cash or future commitment is calculated.

The central idea

Match the service period before comparing costs. An annual equivalent can standardize a repeated-cycle calculation, while purchase dates still require their own cash.

01

Define the service being compared before annualizing the price

A less expensive durable item may need replacement sooner, while a higher-priced alternative may provide more service years. Comparing only their initial prices leaves the service period unresolved.

This example gives both options the same required function continuously. Option A costs CAD 1,200 at each cycle's start, lasts four complete service years and has CAD 80 of running cost at every year-end. Option B costs CAD 2,000, lasts eight years and has CAD 50 of annual running cost.

The lives are deterministic scenario assumptions, not warranties, observed averages or probabilities of survival. Quality, capacity, convenience and reliability are assumed equivalent solely to isolate the cost arithmetic.

ACCA's equivalent-annual-cost explanation provides the general valuation method. The calculator uses its own amounts and complete transaction schedule, without reproducing the source's machine examples or prescribing a household discount rate.

02

Value each complete service cycle with its own dates

The purchase price is paid immediately. Running cost is paid after each full year of use, including the final service year. It represents the year just completed, rather than an optional overhaul performed after the item is discarded.

At the independently entered 4% effective annual discount assumption, the four-year annuity factor is the sum of the discount factors for year-ends one through four. Option A's one-cycle present cost is its CAD 1,200 price plus the present value of four CAD 80 running-cost payments, approximately CAD 1,490.39.

Option B uses its own eight-year factor. Its CAD 2,000 price plus eight discounted CAD 50 payments gives approximately CAD 2,336.64. Those two present costs cover different lengths of service and cannot answer the equal-service comparison by themselves.

Both cycles end with zero salvage value in this illustration. There is no resale receipt, tax depreciation, grant or borrowing fee. A real item with a different residual value or cost pattern would need the corresponding dated cash flow.

03

Convert present cost into a level year-end annual equivalent

An annuity factor converts a constant year-end annual amount into present value. Dividing one cycle's present cost by its own factor reverses that calculation and produces an equivalent annual cost.

The default annual equivalents are approximately CAD 410.59 for A and CAD 347.06 for B. They compare the cost of one year of the defined equal service under the selected valuation and repetition assumptions.

The difference does not mean a seller accepts an annual payment of CAD 347.06 for B. The actual CAD 2,000 purchase is still due immediately. The annual equivalent is a valuation transformation, not a financing installment, accounting depreciation charge or required contribution to a replacement fund.

At zero discount, the formula simplifies to purchase price divided by service years plus annual running cost. With a positive discount assumption, simply dividing the present cost by the number of years would not preserve the present value of a year-end payment stream.

04

Recheck the result over a common complete service horizon

The default common horizon is eight years. A completes two four-year cycles, while B completes one eight-year cycle. A is purchased at time zero and again at year four. B is purchased once at time zero.

Both pay running cost for every completed service year through year eight. At year four, A's running cost for the completed year and its replacement purchase share the same transaction date. At year eight, running costs still apply, but neither option buys a replacement for service beyond the comparison window.

The present cost over those same eight years is approximately CAD 2,764.38 for A and CAD 2,336.64 for B. Each equals its annual-equivalent cost multiplied by the eight-year annuity factor. This independent repeated-calendar calculation checks that the annualized comparison covers equal service.

When the two selected lives do not divide each other, the tool uses their least common multiple. For example, seven- and eight-year lives create a fifty-six-year comparison. That is a conditional arithmetic device, not a forecast that identical items and unchanged prices will actually be available for fifty-six years.

05

Keep the lumpy cash schedule beside the annual equivalent

The cumulative cash chart preserves the purchase and year-end payment dates. It is undiscounted. At the default eight-year endpoint, A has paid CAD 3,040 and B CAD 2,400, while their time-zero present costs are lower because later outflows are discounted.

B still needs CAD 800 more at the initial purchase date. A lower annual-equivalent cost or lower long-horizon present cost does not supply that extra opening cash or establish that the purchase is affordable.

The chart includes no income, bank balance or financing. A separate funding calendar would need the household's resources, payment obligations and any actual credit terms. It would also need to confirm when future replacement money becomes accessible.

A shorter intended ownership period can change the comparison. If the service ends before the item finishes its life, the remaining value, disposal proceeds and whether replacement is needed must be specified. The repeated complete-cycle result should not silently substitute for that limited-horizon question.

06

Test the price and life assumptions that drive the apparent saving

The matrix varies B's price and service life while retaining B's annual running cost, the discount assumption and all of A's selected terms. Every cell reports B's annual equivalent minus A's. A negative value is a lower modeled annual cost for B; it does not guarantee service quality or available cash.

Shortening B's assumed life can reverse a comparison that initially favored it. So can changing its price or running cost. A lifespan claim deserves evidence rather than being chosen to justify an already preferred purchase.

The model repeats identical cycles at constant nominal prices and running costs. It has no inflation, technological change, downtime or uncertain failure. Costs and the discount assumption share that stated nominal basis; the calculator does not mix inflation-linked bills with a real rate.

Use the annual equivalent to understand the conditional cost comparison, then restore the details that matter to the actual decision: required service, supported life range, all cash costs, residual value, intended horizon and funding dates. The four charts keep equal-service valuation and the real shape of payments visible together.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All prices, lives, running costs and discount assumptions are hypothetical. Each option is assumed to provide equivalent service and repeat identically, with zero salvage value. No product lifespan, required saving amount or personal affordability is established. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
